claim: The Arabidopsis circadian clock orchestrates gene regulation across the day/night cycle.
source: The Arabidopsis circadian clock orchestrates gene regulation across the day/night cycle.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the manuscript's introduction and general scientific knowledge.

claim: A multiple feedback loop circuit has been shown to generate the 24-hr rhythm in Arabidopsis.
source: Although a multiple feedback loop circuit has been shown to generate the 24-hr rhythm, it remains unclear how robust the clock is in individual cells, or how clock timing is coordinated across the plant.
evidence: This statement references established models of the circadian clock, as supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: It remains unclear how robust the clock is in individual cells.
source: Although a multiple feedback loop circuit has been shown to generate the 24-hr rhythm, it remains unclear how robust the clock is in individual cells, or how clock timing is coordinated across the plant.
evidence: This is a research gap identified by the authors, which their study aims to address.

claim: It remains unclear how clock timing is coordinated across the plant.
source: Although a multiple feedback loop circuit has been shown to generate the 24-hr rhythm, it remains unclear how robust the clock is in individual cells, or how clock timing is coordinated across the plant.
evidence: This is a research gap identified by the authors, which their study aims to address.

claim: Single cell oscillations in Arabidopsis are robust.
source: Our data reveal robust single cell oscillations, albeit desynchronised.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental data.

claim: Single cell oscillations in Arabidopsis are desynchronised.
source: Our data reveal robust single cell oscillations, albeit desynchronised.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental data.

claim: There are two waves of clock activity in Arabidopsis roots: one going down and one up the root.
source: In particular, we observe two waves of clock activity; one going down, and one up the root.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental observations.

claim: There is evidence of cell-to-cell coupling of the clock, especially in the root tip.
source: We also find evidence of cell-to-cell coupling of the clock, especially in the root tip.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' analysis of single cell data.

claim: Cell-to-cell coupling and measured period differences between cells can generate the observed waves.
source: A simple model shows that cell-to-cell coupling and our measured period differences between cells can generate the observed waves.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' modeling results.

claim: The Arabidopsis clock has multiple coordination points, unlike the centralised mammalian clock.
source: Our results reveal the spatial structure of the plant clock and suggest that unlike the centralised mammalian clock, the Arabidopsis clock has multiple coordination points.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental findings and comparison to mammalian systems.

claim: The circadian clock controls gene expression throughout the day and night in most organisms, from single cell photosynthetic bacteria to mammals.
source: The circadian clock controls gene expression throughout the day and night in most organisms, from single cell photosynthetic bacteria to mammals (Bell-Pedersen et al., 2005; Dunlap and Loros, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A core circuit that generates circadian rhythm has been elucidated and shown to oscillate in single cells.
source: In many cases, a core circuit that generates this rhythm has been elucidated and been shown to oscillate in single cells.
evidence: This is general knowledge in the field of circadian biology.

claim: In multi-cellular organisms, single cell rhythms can be integrated to allow a coordinated response to the environment.
source: In multi-cellular organisms, these single cell rhythms can be integrated to allow a coordinated response to the environment (Bell-Pedersen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mammals achieve coordinated circadian response by driving oscillations in peripheral tissues from a central pacemaker in the brain, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).
source: Mammals achieve this by driving oscillations in peripheral tissues from a central pacemaker in the brain, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) (Pando et al., 2002; Reppert and Weaver, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Arabidopsis circadian clock generates a 24 hr rhythm in multiple key processes, including stomata opening, photosynthesis, and hypocotyl elongation.
source: The Arabidopsis circadian clock generates a 24 hr rhythm in multiple key processes, including stomata opening, photosynthesis, and hypocotyl elongation (Hsu and Harmer, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A hierarchical structure for the plant clock has recently been proposed, similar to that for the mammalian clock, where the shoot apex clock drives the rhythms in the root.
source: A hierarchical structure for the plant clock has recently been proposed, similar to that for the mammalian clock, where the shoot apex clock drives the rhythms in the root (Takahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Experiments using a luciferase reporter for clock activity have shown waves of clock gene expression in leaves.
source: For example, experiments using a luciferase reporter for clock activity have shown waves of clock gene expression in leaves (Fukuda et al., 2007; Wenden et al., 2012), as well as striped expression patterns in roots (Fukuda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Experiments using a luciferase reporter for clock activity have shown striped expression patterns in roots.
source: For example, experiments using a luciferase reporter for clock activity have shown waves of clock gene expression in leaves (Fukuda et al., 2007; Wenden et al., 2012), as well as striped expression patterns in roots (Fukuda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A genetic circuit consisting of multiple coupled feedback loops has been proposed to generate the 24-hr rhythm in Arabidopsis.
source: Through integration of data from whole plant studies, a genetic circuit consisting of multiple coupled feedback loops has been proposed to generate the 24-hr rhythm (Fogelmark and Troein, 2014; Pokhilko et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Simulations of the circadian clock network display stable oscillations.
source: Simulations of this network display stable oscillations (Figure 1a), although experimental measurements of clock rhythms under constant conditions often display damped rhythms (Figure 1b) (Gould et al., 2013; Locke et al., 2005; Locke et al., 2006; Salomé and McClung, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1a and citations to previous literature.

claim: Experimental measurements of clock rhythms under constant conditions often display damped rhythms.
source: Simulations of this network display stable oscillations (Figure 1a), although experimental measurements of clock rhythms under constant conditions often display damped rhythms (Figure 1b) (Gould et al., 2013; Locke et al., 2005; Locke et al., 2006; Salomé and McClung, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1b and citations to previous literature.

claim: Damping at the whole plant level could be due to the clock circuit in all individual cells damping.
source: This damping at the whole plant level could be due to the clock circuit in all individual cells damping (top, Figure 1c), or to cells desynchronising due to different intrinsic periods or phases (Guerriero et al., 2012; Komin et al., 2011) (bottom, Figure 1c), or cells desynchronising due to stochasticity in clock activity (Guerriero et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis presented by the authors, supported by references to previous literature and Figure 1c.

claim: Damping at the whole plant level could be due to cells desynchronising due to different intrinsic periods or phases.
source: This damping at the whole plant level could be due to the clock circuit in all individual cells damping (top, Figure 1c), or to cells desynchronising due to different intrinsic periods or phases (Guerriero et al., 2012; Komin et al., 2011) (bottom, Figure 1c), or cells desynchronising due to stochasticity in clock activity (Guerriero et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis presented by the authors, supported by references to previous literature and Figure 1c.

claim: Damping at the whole plant level could be due to cells desynchronising due to stochasticity in clock activity.
source: This damping at the whole plant level could be due to the clock circuit in all individual cells damping (top, Figure 1c), or to cells desynchronising due to different intrinsic periods or phases (Guerriero et al., 2012; Komin et al., 2011) (bottom, Figure 1c), or cells desynchronising due to stochasticity in clock activity (Guerriero et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis presented by the authors, supported by references to previous literature and Figure 1c.

claim: Previous studies have attempted to measure the clock in Arabidopsis at single-cell resolution, but have focused on specific parts of the plant for short time series.
source: Previous studies have attempted to measure the clock in Arabidopsis at single-cell resolution; however, these have focused on specific parts of the plant for short time series (Takahashi et al., 2015; Yakir et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Current models of the clock predict undamped oscillations.
source: (a), Current models of the clock (Pokhilko et al., 2012) predict undamped oscillations.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1a and a citation to a previous model.

claim: CCA1:LUC expression bulk averaged over multiple seedlings shows damping clock oscillations.
source: (b), CCA1:LUC expression bulk averaged over multiple seedlings shows damping clock oscillations (mean ± s.e.m.; n = 32 seedlings).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1b and experimental data.

claim: The emission spectra from 450 to 650 nm for the CCA1-YFP in each tissue is consistent with the known YFP emission spectrum.
source: (a) The emission spectra from 450 to 650 nm for the CCA1-YFP in each tissue is consistent with the known YFP emission spectrum.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and experimental data.

claim: Transformation of the cca1-11 mutant with CCA1::CCA1-YFP construct has rescued the short period clock phenotype of cca1 in the WT CCA1-YFP construct.
source: (b, c), Transformation of the cca1-11 mutant with CCA1::CCA1-YFP construct has rescued the short period clock phenotype of cca1 in the WT CCA1-YFP construct (a), and produced a long period line in the CCA1-long CCA1-YFP construct (b) (mean ± s.e.m.; n represents groups of seedlings).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c and experimental data.

claim: Transformation of the cca1-11 mutant with CCA1::CCA1-YFP construct produced a long period line in the CCA1-long CCA1-YFP construct.
source: (b, c), Transformation of the cca1-11 mutant with CCA1::CCA1-YFP construct has rescued the short period clock phenotype of cca1 in the WT CCA1-YFP construct (a), and produced a long period line in the CCA1-long CCA1-YFP construct (b) (mean ± s.e.m.; n represents groups of seedlings).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c and experimental data.

claim: CCA1-YFP is expressed in the nucleus of the root tip, root, hypocotyl and cotyledon.
source: (d), Orthographic projection of a z stack of a cca1-11 CCA1::CCA1-YFP construct with intervals of 2 µm across 60 slices. CCA1-YFP is expressed in the nucleus of the root tip, root, hypocotyl and cotyledon.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and experimental data.

claim: Oscillations could be observed in all tissues.
source: Oscillations could be observed in all tissues, with most cells displaying circadian rhythms (see Figure 1—source datas 1 and 2 for percentage of cells scored rhythmic for each plant section).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental observations and data.

claim: Most cells display circadian rhythms.
source: Oscillations could be observed in all tissues, with most cells displaying circadian rhythms (see Figure 1—source datas 1 and 2 for percentage of cells scored rhythmic for each plant section).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental observations and data.

claim: Analysis of single cell oscillation amplitudes during the course of the movie revealed stable oscillations, with only a slight reduction in median oscillation amplitude in the root.
source: Analysis of single cell oscillation amplitudes during the course of the movie revealed stable oscillations, with only a slight reduction in median oscillation amplitude in the root (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 6 and experimental data.

claim: Neither the strong damping at the tissue level in the root, nor the damping observed at the plant level, can be explained by individual cells losing rhythmicity.
source: Neither the strong damping at the tissue level in the root (Figure 1g), nor the damping observed at the plant level (Figure 1a), can be explained by individual cells losing rhythmicity (Figure 1h, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data and analysis.

claim: The hypocotyl and cotyledon were the most synchronised, with the amplitude of the mean trace nearly equalling the median amplitude of the individual cell time-series.
source: The hypocotyl and cotyledon were the most synchronised, with the amplitude of the mean trace nearly equalling the median amplitude of the individual cell time-series (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 2a and supplementary figures, and experimental data.

claim: The hypocotyl and cotyledon rhythms exhibited low period variability both within and between time traces, indicating a high level of robustness.
source: The hypocotyl and cotyledon rhythms also exhibited low period variability both within and between time traces, indicating a high level of robustness (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplements 1b and 2b).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 2b and supplementary figures, and experimental data.

claim: The root displayed significant desynchronisation, with the amplitude of the mean trace lower than the median amplitude of the individual cell traces.
source: However, the root displayed significant desynchronisation, with the amplitude of the mean trace lower than the median amplitude of the individual cell traces (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplements 1a and 2a), with higher variability in period within and between single cell lineages (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplements 1b and 2b).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 2a,b and supplementary figures, and experimental data.

claim: The root displayed higher variability in period within and between single cell lineages.
source: However, the root displayed significant desynchronisation, with the amplitude of the mean trace lower than the median amplitude of the individual cell traces (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplements 1a and 2a), with higher variability in period within and between single cell lineages (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplements 1b and 2b).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 2b and supplementary figures, and experimental data.

claim: Simulations of the stochastic model display greater desynchronisation as the system size is reduced.
source: Simulations of the stochastic model of the Arabidopsis gene network (Guerriero et al., 2012) display greater desynchronisation as the system size, effectively the simulated number of molecules in the cell, is reduced (Figure 2c–e).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 2c-e and modeling results.

claim: The lower the molecule number, the more desynchronisation at the single cell level, and the more damping of the mean expression.
source: The lower the molecule number, the more desynchronisation at the single cell level, and the more damping of the mean expression (red line, Figure 2c), even though the individual traces do not display a damped rhythm.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 2c and modeling results.

claim: Previously the system size was estimated to be on the order of 100 molecules per cell in order for the desynchronisation observed in whole plant measurements to be explained solely by noise.
source: Previously the system size was estimated to be on the order of 100 molecules per cell (bottom panel, Figure 2c) in order for the desynchronisation observed in whole plant measurements to be explained solely by noise (Guerriero et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and reference to Figure 2c.

claim: The single cell rhythms detected in the hypocotyl and cotyledon have a lower period variability than a system size of 100 and behave closer to a system size of 1000.
source: The single cell rhythms that we detect in the hypocotyl and cotyledon have a lower period variability (Figure 2b) than a system size of 100 and in fact behave closer to a system size of 1000 (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claim: The hypocotyl and cotyledon have a smaller difference between the amplitude of the mean trace compared to the median amplitude of the individual cell time-series than a system size of 100, and behave closer to a system size of 1000.
source: The hypocotyl and cotyledon also have a smaller difference between the amplitude of the mean trace (green line) compared to the median amplitude of the individual cell time-series (red line) (Figure 2a) than a system size of 100 (Figure 2d), and again behaves closer to a system size of 1000 (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claim: The level of desynchronisation observed in the root and root tip behave more like a simulated system size of 100.
source: The level of desynchronisation observed in the root and root tip, however, behave more like a simulated system size of 100 (Figure 2a–e).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claim: Similar CCA1-YFP expression levels are observed across the plant.
source: Similar CCA1-YFP expression levels are observed across the plant (Figure 2f,g), so it is unlikely that this lack of robustness is due solely to a change of total molecule number for the clock system in different parts of the plant.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 2f,g and experimental data.

claim: It is unlikely that the lack of robustness in the root is due solely to a change of total molecule number for the clock system in different parts of the plant.
source: Similar CCA1-YFP expression levels are observed across the plant (Figure 2f,g), so it is unlikely that this lack of robustness is due solely to a change of total molecule number for the clock system in different parts of the plant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data.

claim: The amplitude and expression levels of the single cell oscillations in the root tip are high compared to other sections across the plant.
source: In fact the amplitude and expression levels of the single cell oscillations in the root tip are high compared to other sections across the plant (Figure 2f,g and Figure 2—figure supplements 1a,c–d and 2a,c–d).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 2f,g and supplementary figures, and experimental data.

claim: The upper sections of the root displayed longer periods than the rest of the plant.
source: The upper sections of the root displayed longer periods than the rest of the plant, as reported previously for the whole root (James et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental data and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Very fast rhythms are observed in the root tip.
source: However, we observed very fast rhythms in the root tip (Figure 3a,b), which is also the section with very high expression rhythms (Figure 2f,g).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3a,b and experimental data.

claim: The root tip is the section with very high expression rhythms.
source: However, we observed very fast rhythms in the root tip (Figure 3a,b), which is also the section with very high expression rhythms (Figure 2f,g).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 2f,g and experimental data.

claim: There is no evidence of phase resetting in the root tip in this study.
source: Although we do not observe evidence of phase resetting in the root tip, as proposed in an earlier luciferase study (Fukuda et al., 2012), this could be due to our different growth conditions and stage of plant development.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of a finding in the authors' data.

claim: The absence of phase resetting in the root tip could be due to different growth conditions and stage of plant development compared to an earlier study.
source: Although we do not observe evidence of phase resetting in the root tip, as proposed in an earlier luciferase study (Fukuda et al., 2012), this could be due to our different growth conditions and stage of plant development.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors to explain a discrepancy with previous literature.

claim: Plots of period in the z direction in each section do not reveal any discernible pattern.
source: Plots of period in the z direction in each section do not reveal any discernible pattern (Figure 3c,d, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3c,d and supplementary figures, and experimental data.

claim: The differences in rhythms observed are not restricted to a specific cell type.
source: This suggests that the differences in rhythms we observe are not restricted to a specific cell type.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data.

claim: The clock peaks earlier in the hypocotyl than in the cotyledon.
source: Examination of the clock phase between 48 and 72 hr reveals that the clock peaks earlier in the hypocotyl (mean phase in upper hypocotyl 51.2 ± 1.1h, mean phase in lower hypocotyl 52.1 ± 1.5h) than in the cotyledon (mean phase 55.6 ± 2.3h) (Figure 3f–h).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3f-h and experimental data.

claim: From the top of the root the phase of the clock is shifted to later in the day as you go down the root.
source: From the top of the root the phase of the clock is shifted to later in the day as you go down the root (upper root mean phase 56.6 ± 4.5h) (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3h and experimental data.

claim: From the root tip the phase of the clock is shifted to later in the day as you go up.
source: However, from the root tip (mean phase 56.2 ± 5.0h) the phase of the clock is shifted to later in the day as you go up (lower root phase 58.0 ± 4.4h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Two waves are generated in the montages of clock gene expression, one going up and one going down the root.
source: This generates two waves in the montages of clock gene expression, one going up and one going down the root (Figure 3e; Video 1; Figure 2—figure supplements 1g and 2g).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3e, Video 1, and supplementary figures, and experimental data.

claim: At each y position in the root, the phases are more variable than in the rest of the plant.
source: At each y position in the root, the phases are also more variable than in the rest of the plant, with a standard deviation of phases of ±5.0 hr in the root tip compared to ±1.1 hr in the hypocotyl for phases occurring between 48 and 72 hr (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3h and experimental data.

claim: The damped mean rhythm of clock activity observed in the root is caused by the averaging of two waves of gene expression that have a broad distribution of phases.
source: Thus, the damped mean rhythm of clock activity we observed in the root (Figure 1g) is caused by the averaging of these two waves of gene expression that have a broad distribution of phases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data and analysis.

claim: Qualitatively similar waves were observed in luciferase reporter lines for the clock genes PSEUDO-RESPONSE REGULATOR 9, CCA1 and GIGANTEA.
source: We observed qualitatively similar waves in luciferase reporter lines for the clock genes PSEUDO-RESPONSE REGULATOR 9 (Ito et al., 2003) (Figure 3i; Video 4), CCA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) and GIGANTEA (Park et al., 1999) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that our results are a general property of the clock.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3i, Video 4, and supplementary figures, and experimental data.

claim: The observed waves are a general property of the clock.
source: We observed qualitatively similar waves in luciferase reporter lines for the clock genes PSEUDO-RESPONSE REGULATOR 9 (Ito et al., 2003) (Figure 3i; Video 4), CCA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) and GIGANTEA (Park et al., 1999) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that our results are a general property of the clock.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data.

claim: Signs of coupling were observed across the plant, with the strongest evidence for coupling in the root tip.
source: We observed signs of coupling across the plant, with the strongest evidence for coupling in the root tip, where the order parameter actually increased with time (Figure 3j and Figure 3—figure supplement 2–4).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3j and supplementary figures, and experimental data.

claim: The order parameter increased with time in the root tip.
source: We observed signs of coupling across the plant, with the strongest evidence for coupling in the root tip, where the order parameter actually increased with time (Figure 3j and Figure 3—figure supplement 2–4).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3j and supplementary figures, and experimental data.

claim: The strongest coupling occurred where cell density was highest.
source: Interestingly, this occurred where cell density was highest, as observed in cultured SCN cells (Aton et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental data and a citation to previous literature.

claim: A simple model where cells are described by coupled oscillators with different periods can generate waves of gene expression up and down the root.
source: To investigate the mechanism for the waves of clock gene expression in the root we developed a simple mathematical model where the cells are described by coupled oscillators with different periods, as informed by the data (Figure 3k).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3k and modeling results.

claim: The simple model can produce a bow wave in the space-time plot, similar to that observed experimentally.
source: This simple model can generate waves of gene expression up and down the root that produce a bow wave in the space-time plot (Figure 3k), similar to that observed experimentally (Figure 3h,i).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3k, 3h, and 3i, and modeling results.

claim: Tissue specific differences in the phases and robustness of the clock in Arabidopsis have been revealed by single cell measurements.
source: Our single cell measurements have revealed tissue specific differences in the phases and robustness of the clock in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is a summary of the authors' findings.

claim: The observed differences in clock phases and robustness are not restricted to one cell type.
source: These differences are not restricted to one cell type, as similar periods are observed in the z dimension through the plant (Figure 3c,d), suggesting that cells are instead responding to information based on their longitudinal position.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data.

claim: Cells are responding to information based on their longitudinal position.
source: These differences are not restricted to one cell type, as similar periods are observed in the z dimension through the plant (Figure 3c,d), suggesting that cells are instead responding to information based on their longitudinal position.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data.

claim: The observed robust rhythms in the hypocotyl that peak before the cotyledon and the top of the root, with a wave of clock gene expression down the root, fit with a proposed hierarchical structure for the plant clock.
source: The observed robust rhythms in the hypocotyl that peak before the cotyledon and the top of the root, with a wave of clock gene expression down the root, fit with a proposed hierarchical structure for the plant clock, where the shoot apex clock drives the rhythms in the root (Takahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison of the authors' findings to a previously proposed model.

claim: The hierarchical model does not explain the observed short period oscillations in the root tip, or the wave of clock gene expression up from the root tip.
source: However, our results suggest that the structure of the plant clock is more complicated, as this hierarchical model does not explain the observed short period oscillations in the root tip, or the wave of clock gene expression up from the root tip.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data.

claim: The results support a more decentralised model of clock coordination in plants.
source: Our results support a more decentralised model of clock coordination in plants (Endo, 2016; Endo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Earlier studies of the Arabidopsis clock argue either that cellular oscillations are uncoupled, or weakly, but detectably, coupled.
source: Earlier studies of the Arabidopsis clock argue either that cellular oscillations are uncoupled (Thain et al., 2000; Yakir et al., 2011), or weakly, but detectably, coupled (Fukuda et al., 2007; Fukuda et al., 2012; James et al., 2008; Takahashi et al., 2015; Wenden et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Coupling has been detected in Lemna gibba fronds, as examination of a clock bioluminescence reporter with single cell resolution showed weak coupling between individual clock oscillators under constant conditions.
source: Coupling has also been detected in Lemna gibba fronds, as examination of a clock bioluminescence reporter with single cell resolution showed weak coupling between individual clock oscillators under constant conditions (Muranaka and Oyama, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Heterogeneous oscillations in Lemna gibba could be synchronised by light-dark cycles.
source: These heterogeneous oscillations could be synchronised by light-dark cycles (Okada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The single cell approach is consistent with weak coupling across the whole plant but reveals regions with strong local coupling between cells, especially in the root tip.
source: Our single cell approach is consistent with weak coupling across the whole plant but reveals regions with strong local coupling between cells, especially in the root tip, which is sufficient to drive an increase in synchrony with time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data and analysis.

claim: Strong local coupling in the root tip is sufficient to drive an increase in synchrony with time.
source: Our single cell approach is consistent with weak coupling across the whole plant but reveals regions with strong local coupling between cells, especially in the root tip, which is sufficient to drive an increase in synchrony with time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data and analysis.

claim: Cell-cell coupling together with the observed period differences between tissues is sufficient to replicate the decentralised spatial structure of the clock observed experimentally.
source: Our modelling reveals that cell-cell coupling together with the observed period differences between tissues is sufficient to replicate the decentralised spatial structure of the clock that we observe experimentally.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' modeling results.

claim: The simple model offers a qualitative match to data.
source: Our simple model offers a qualitative match to data.
evidence: This is an assessment of the authors' model.

claim: Decentralised coordination could create flexibility and allow parts of the plant to respond differentially to environmental perturbations.
source: Decentralised coordination could create flexibility and allow parts of the plant to respond differentially to environmental perturbations.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the functional implications of their findings.

claim: There is evidence that the root clock may respond differently to light than the shoot.
source: There is already evidence that the root clock may respond differently to light than the shoot (Bordage et al., 2016; Nimmo, 2018), and that the vasculature and epidermal clock regulate distinct physiological processes (Shimizu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The vasculature and epidermal clock regulate distinct physiological processes.
source: There is already evidence that the root clock may respond differently to light than the shoot (Bordage et al., 2016; Nimmo, 2018), and that the vasculature and epidermal clock regulate distinct physiological processes (Shimizu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Initiation of lateral roots triggers the resetting of the clock in the emerging lateral root.
source: It has been recently shown that initiation of lateral roots triggers the resetting of the clock in the emerging lateral root (Voß et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Auxin is proposed to be involved in resetting the clock in lateral roots.
source: In the case of lateral roots, auxin is proposed to be involved in resetting the clock (Voß et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Waves of auxin occur in the root.
source: Waves of auxin also occur in the root (Moreno-Risueno et al., 2010), and it will be interesting to examine if the circadian clock wave is linked to these auxin dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: It will be interesting to examine if the circadian clock wave is linked to auxin dynamics.
source: Waves of auxin also occur in the root (Moreno-Risueno et al., 2010), and it will be interesting to examine if the circadian clock wave is linked to these auxin dynamics.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about future research directions.

claim: An important next step will be to investigate what the coupling signal is for the plant circadian clock.
source: An important next step will be to investigate what the coupling signal is for the plant circadian clock (Covington and Harmer, 2007; Dalchau et al., 2011; Haydon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about future research directions, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The CCA1::CCA1-YFP construct was transformed in cca1-11 (Ws) mutant background.
source: The CCA1::CCA1-YFP construct was transformed in cca1-11 (Ws) mutant background (Hall, 2003).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Homozygous T3 generations of several independent transgenic lines were checked for complementation via delayed fluorescence.
source: Homozygous T3 generations of several independent transgenic lines were checked for complementation via delayed fluorescence (Gould et al., 2009) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, c).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The CCA1::CCA1-YFP expressing line showing full complementation was re-transformed with 35S::H2B-RFP.
source: The CCA1::CCA1-YFP expressing line showing full complementation was then re-transformed with 35S::H2B-RFP which was used for tracking purposes during analysis (Federici et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: A custom developed time-lapse confocal microscope setup was used to carry out time-lapse movies of Arabidopsis seedlings.
source: We carried out time-lapse movies of Arabidopsis seedlings using a custom developed time-lapse confocal microscope setup (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Seedlings were entrained to 12:12 hr light/dark cycles before examining the clock under constant conditions.
source: In order to examine the intrinsic behaviour of the clock we first entrained the seedlings to 12:12 hr light/dark cycles before examining the clock under constant conditions (constant blue light (30 μmol m−2 s−1) and temperature (22°C)).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The method allowed tracking and extraction of fluorescence values from the same individual nuclei over several days.
source: Our method allowed us to track and extract fluorescence values from the same individual nuclei over several days (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: A robust oscillation was observed in the cotyledon, although with slight damping to the amplitude.
source: We observed a robust oscillation in the cotyledon (red line, Figure 1g) and hypocotyl (blue line, Figure 1g), although with slight damping to the amplitude.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1g and experimental data.

claim: A robust oscillation was observed in the hypocotyl, although with slight damping to the amplitude.
source: We observed a robust oscillation in the cotyledon (red line, Figure 1g) and hypocotyl (blue line, Figure 1g), although with slight damping to the amplitude.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1g and experimental data.

claim: Strong damping of the circadian rhythm was observed in the top part of the root.
source: In the top part of the root we observed strong damping of the circadian rhythm (black line, Figure 1g), although the oscillations recovered somewhat in the root tip (grey line, Figure 1g).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1g and experimental data.

claim: The oscillations recovered somewhat in the root tip.
source: In the top part of the root we observed strong damping of the circadian rhythm (black line, Figure 1g), although the oscillations recovered somewhat in the root tip (grey line, Figure 1g).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1g and experimental data.

claim: Three repeat plants showed similar behaviour to the first plant analyzed.
source: Three repeat plants showed similar behaviour (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and experimental data.

claim: Similar behaviour was observed in the CCA1-long reporter line.
source: We also observed similar behaviour in our CCA1-long reporter line (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), showing that our results remain true across a range of clock activity.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and experimental data.

claim: The results remain true across a range of clock activity.
source: We also observed similar behaviour in our CCA1-long reporter line (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), showing that our results remain true across a range of clock activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data.

claim: The mean phase in upper hypocotyl is 51.2 ± 1.1h.
source: Examination of the clock phase between 48 and 72 hr reveals that the clock peaks earlier in the hypocotyl (mean phase in upper hypocotyl 51.2 ± 1.1h, mean phase in lower hypocotyl 52.1 ± 1.5h) than in the cotyledon (mean phase 55.6 ± 2.3h) (Figure 3f–h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The mean phase in lower hypocotyl is 52.1 ± 1.5h.
source: Examination of the clock phase between 48 and 72 hr reveals that the clock peaks earlier in the hypocotyl (mean phase in upper hypocotyl 51.2 ± 1.1h, mean phase in lower hypocotyl 52.1 ± 1.5h) than in the cotyledon (mean phase 55.6 ± 2.3h) (Figure 3f–h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The mean phase in cotyledon is 55.6 ± 2.3h.
source: Examination of the clock phase between 48 and 72 hr reveals that the clock peaks earlier in the hypocotyl (mean phase in upper hypocotyl 51.2 ± 1.1h, mean phase in lower hypocotyl 52.1 ± 1.5h) than in the cotyledon (mean phase 55.6 ± 2.3h) (Figure 3f–h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The upper root mean phase is 56.6 ± 4.5h.
source: From the top of the root the phase of the clock is shifted to later in the day as you go down the root (upper root mean phase 56.6 ± 4.5h) (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The root tip mean phase is 56.2 ± 5.0h.
source: However, from the root tip (mean phase 56.2 ± 5.0h) the phase of the clock is shifted to later in the day as you go up (lower root phase 58.0 ± 4.4h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The lower root phase is 58.0 ± 4.4h.
source: However, from the root tip (mean phase 56.2 ± 5.0h) the phase of the clock is shifted to later in the day as you go up (lower root phase 58.0 ± 4.4h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The standard deviation of phases in the root tip is ±5.0 hr for phases occurring between 48 and 72 hr.
source: At each y position in the root, the phases are also more variable than in the rest of the plant, with a standard deviation of phases of ±5.0 hr in the root tip compared to ±1.1 hr in the hypocotyl for phases occurring between 48 and 72 hr (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The standard deviation of phases in the hypocotyl is ±1.1 hr for phases occurring between 48 and 72 hr.
source: At each y position in the root, the phases are also more variable than in the rest of the plant, with a standard deviation of phases of ±5.0 hr in the root tip compared to ±1.1 hr in the hypocotyl for phases occurring between 48 and 72 hr (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The shoot apical meristem has a high cell density like the root tip.
source: In the future, it will be interesting to examine whether the shoot apical meristem, which has a high cell density like the root tip and has been shown to be coupled when excised from the plant, has a similarly high coupling strength given its role in driving rhythms in the shoot (Takahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is implied by the comparison made by the authors.

claim: In the future it will be interesting to develop more mechanistic models of the plant circadian clock at the single cell level.
source: In the future it will be interesting to develop more mechanistic models of the plant circadian clock at the single cell level, as has been done at the bulk level previously (Fogelmark and Troein, 2014; Guerriero et al., 2012; Locke et al., 2005; Locke et al., 2006; Pokhilko et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about future research directions.

claim: Currently estimations of clock periods from single cells are from the intact plant, and so will include the effects of cell-cell coupling.
source: One barrier to achieving this is that currently our estimations of clock periods from single cells are from the intact plant, and so will include the effects of cell-cell coupling.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.
